header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking

related.why: Another upper GI cancer history built on NG12

brief.scenario: Mr Derek Walsh, 64, has been referred by his GP with three months of indigestion.
brief.task: Take a focused history. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise your history, then asked about differential diagnosis, investigation and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Indigestion at 64 is a cancer question until the alarm features are asked and answered.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating it as reflux because the pharmacy omeprazole partly helped.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Open question, then quantify the weight loss: how much, over how long?

grid.label: Opening and rapport
grid.fail: Launches into closed questions without introduction or an open question.
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, asks an open question and lets him finish.
grid.high: Picks up his cue about his wife early and signposts: "I'll come back to that."

grid.label: Presenting complaint
grid.fail: Records "indigestion" without site, timing or relation to food.
grid.pass: Site, character, relation to meals, duration, relieving factors; early satiety and vomiting.
grid.high: Quantifies weight loss in kilograms over a time period, and asks what the omeprazole changed.

grid.label: Alarm features (safety-critical)
grid.borderline: Asks about weight loss but not dysphagia or bleeding.
grid.pass: Asks directly about dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, haematemesis, melaena and symptoms of anaemia.
grid.high: Asks about a lump in the abdomen, and states each negative back to him to confirm it.

grid.label: Drugs and risk factors
grid.pass: Asks about NSAIDs, aspirin, anticoagulants and over-the-counter PPIs; smoking, alcohol and family history.
grid.high: Adds other culprit drugs (bisphosphonates, steroids, calcium antagonists) and any previous endoscopy.

grid.label: Ideas, concerns, expectations
grid.fail: Doesn't ask what he thinks is wrong.
grid.pass: Asks what he thinks is causing it, what worries him, and what he hopes for today.
grid.high: Names his fear of cancer honestly and links his carer role to the plan.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.fail: Retells the history in order, or gives no working diagnosis.
grid.pass: Concise summary with key positives and negatives, and a working diagnosis with differential.
grid.high: Leads with the alarm features and says gastric or oesophageal cancer must be excluded.

grid.label: Referral and investigation
grid.fail: Plans a longer PPI trial or H. pylori testing first.
grid.pass: Meets NG12 suspected cancer criteria (55 or over, weight loss, dyspepsia); books the urgent OGD directly.
grid.high: Says the suspected cancer pathway aims for diagnosis or exclusion within 28 days; adds FBC for anaemia.

grid.label: Management and safety-netting
grid.fail: Continues the ibuprofen, or gives no safety-net advice.
grid.pass: Stops the NSAID; safety-nets for vomiting blood, black stools or swallowing difficulty.
grid.high: Says acute GI bleeding means same-day referral, and considers cardiac or biliary causes.

pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Shah, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? Tell me about the problem in your own words.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Where is the pain? Is it linked to eating? How long has it been going on? Do you feel full quickly? Any vomiting?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you lost weight? Any difficulty swallowing? Have you vomited blood or passed black stools? Have you been more tired or breathless?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What medicines do you take, including from the chemist? Any ibuprofen or aspirin? Do you smoke or drink? Any stomach cancer in the family?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What do you think is going on? Is anything worrying you? What were you hoping for today?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Walsh is 64, with three months of epigastric pain, early satiety and 7 kg weight loss, taking ibuprofen and over-the-counter omeprazole. No dysphagia or bleeding. I'm worried about gastric cancer; the differential is peptic ulcer or NSAID gastropathy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: He meets the NG12 suspected cancer criteria: 55 or over with weight loss and dyspepsia. I'd book an urgent OGD myself. I'd stop the ibuprofen and tell him to come back at once if he vomits blood, has black stools or can't swallow.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Shah, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? Tell me what's been happening. [Hears that he cares for his wife.] That sounds hard; I'll come back to that.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: How much weight, and over what time? And what difference has the omeprazole made?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any lump you've felt in your tummy? So, to check: no swallowing trouble, no blood in the vomit, no black stools?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any tablets for your bones, steroids, or blood pressure tablets like amlodipine? Have you ever had a camera test?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You mentioned your friend. Are you worried this could be cancer? I'll be honest: we need to rule that out quickly. Who looks after your wife if you have tests?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mr Walsh, 64, has alarm features: 7 kg weight loss in three months with dyspepsia and early satiety. He takes ibuprofen and has self-medicated with omeprazole. He has no dysphagia or GI bleeding. Gastric or oesophageal cancer must be excluded; peptic ulcer is the main alternative.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He meets the NG12 criteria, so he stays on the suspected cancer pathway, which aims to diagnose or exclude cancer within 28 days. I'd book an urgent OGD myself and check a full blood count for anaemia. I'd stop the ibuprofen. Vomiting blood or melaena would mean same-day referral. I'd keep cardiac and biliary causes in the differential.

failures.move: Not asking about dysphagia, haematemesis or melaena.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: misses the features that change the referral route and urgency.
Over-the-counter ibuprofen and omeprazole go unrecorded: the likely ulcer cause is missed, and so is a PPI that can ease symptoms and delay a cancer diagnosis.
His fear of cancer and his caring role stay hidden, and both affect whether he attends.

failures.move: Extending the PPI trial because symptoms partly improved.
failures.consequence: Partial response does not exclude cancer; he already meets the NG12 suspected cancer criteria.

recovery.when: You forgot to ask about bleeding
recovery.line: Before we finish, have you vomited blood or noticed black, tarry stools?

recovery.when: He asks directly if it's cancer
recovery.line: It's one of the things we need to rule out, and that's why I'm arranging tests quickly.

knowledge.fact: NG12 suspected cancer pathway criteria for oesophageal or stomach cancer (primary care referral): dysphagia, or age 55+ with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia (1.2.1, 1.2.7; amended 2025 from direct-access endoscopy).
Non-urgent direct-access endoscopy at 55+ for treatment-resistant dyspepsia, or upper abdominal pain with low haemoglobin (1.2.3, 1.2.9).
Unexplained weight loss over 5% in 6 months at 60+: assess for other features, then urgent investigation or referral (1.13.2, 2026).
Review culprit drugs; suspend NSAIDs in people needing referral (1.3.2).
With alarm symptoms, a PPI can ease symptoms and delay a cancer diagnosis: exclude malignancy.

recall.think: Gastric or oesophageal cancer; upper GI bleeding.
recall.say: "He meets suspected cancer criteria; I'll book an urgent OGD."

numbers.meaning: with weight loss and dyspepsia: suspected cancer criteria
suspected cancer pathway: diagnosis or exclusion

recall.finish: Urgent OGD on the suspected cancer pathway; stop NSAID; safety-net.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9-minute stations with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself and confirm identity at every station

sources.name: NICE NG12: Suspected cancer: recognition and referral
sources.supports: Suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal (1.2.1) and stomach cancer (1.2.7), amended May 2025; non-urgent direct-access endoscopy (1.2.3, 1.2.9); unexplained weight loss at 60+ (1.13.2, April 2026); suspected cancer pathway definition (28 days)

sources.name: NICE CG184: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia in adults: investigation and management
sources.supports: Same-day specialist referral for dyspepsia with significant acute GI bleeding (1.3.1); review drugs that cause dyspepsia and suspend NSAIDs in people needing referral (1.3.2); consider cardiac or biliary disease (1.3.3)

sources.name: Omeprazole: Summary of Product Characteristics (electronic medicines compendium), section 4.4
sources.supports: With alarm symptoms (weight loss, recurrent vomiting, dysphagia, haematemesis, melaena), exclude malignancy: treatment may ease symptoms and delay diagnosis

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Mr Walsh. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: You are Derek Walsh, 64, a retired bus driver. Opening line: "It's this indigestion, doctor. It just won't go." Emotional state: matter-of-fact, but quietly frightened. Volunteer only that it's a gnawing pain under the ribs after meals for three months. Release the other facts only when asked the right question (see reveals). Hidden concern: a friend died of stomach cancer last year; you only say so if asked what worries you. You care for your wife, who has MS; mention "I look after my wife" early as a cue, and expand only if the candidate comes back to it. Expectation: "a stronger tablet".

reveals.finding: "I feel full after half a plate. Sometimes I bring food back up."
"My trousers are loose. About 7 kilos since the summer" (three months; was 82 kg).

reveals.trigger: Asks about swallowing, vomiting blood or black stools

reveals.finding: "I get puffed on the stairs lately."
Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for his knee for a year; omeprazole from the chemist for two months, which "takes the edge off".
Smoked 20 a day for 40 years, stopped 5 years ago; 10 units a week; no family history of cancer.
"My mate Tony had this. It was stomach cancer."
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history."

push.question: What is your differential?
push.expect: Gastric or oesophageal cancer; peptic ulcer; NSAID gastropathy.

push.question: What would you arrange, and how fast?
push.expect: Meets NG12 suspected cancer criteria (55+, weight loss, dyspepsia); candidate books urgent OGD; 28-day diagnosis standard.

push.question: What would you do about his medicines?
push.expect: Stop the NSAID; safety-net for bleeding and dysphagia.

curveballs.prompt: He mentions he passed a black, sticky stool yesterday.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible upper GI bleed: same-day assessment, not an outpatient referral.

curveballs.prompt: "Can't I just have a stronger tablet?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Tablets may ease symptoms but won't tell us the cause; he needs a camera test first.

curveballs.prompt: The omeprazole has made him much better. Does he still need the OGD?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes. Symptom response doesn't exclude cancer, and he meets the criteria on age and weight loss; he still needs the urgent OGD.
